title: Five minutes outside the bakery

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Have you ever paid a fine? Guess: why did Sam get one last week?

chapters.title: A forty-manat ticket
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 1 SCENE: a sunny Baku street outside a small bakery, a red-haired bearded man looking in shock at a parking ticket under the wiper of his car, a no-parking sign beside it

chapters.title: The garage
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 2 SCENE: a garden behind a house, a bald older man with a grey moustache and a checked shirt standing proudly next to a small new garage while a serious inspector with a clipboard frowns, NOT the podcast hosts

chapters.title: The witness
chapters.prompt: CHAPTER 3 SCENE: a city street, a woman with round glasses and a lavender sweater talking calmly to a police officer, a bicycle lying on the road and a young cyclist sitting unhurt on the pavement

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is rules and laws. And I have a confession: last week I got a fine.
A fine? For what?
Parking. I left my car outside the bakery for five minutes. When I came back, there was a ticket on the window. Forty manat.
[laugh] Five minutes! Was it forbidden to park there?
There was a sign, yes. I just didn't see it. So it was fair, I suppose.
In Baku the cameras see everything. You can't get away with it any more.
In England it's the same. But some people still try to bend the rules a little.
Like my neighbour, Mr Aliyev. He wanted to build a garage in his garden, but he didn't have a permit.
Oh no. What happened?
He built it anyway. Then an inspector came, and he had to take it down.
Ouch. So he didn't get away with it.
No. And now he says every law in this country is too strict. [chuckle]
Have you ever been a witness to anything?
Once. I saw a small accident — a car hit a bicycle. The police asked me what I saw.
Was it scary?
A little. But the cyclist was okay, and I just told the truth.
Good for you. Some rules I don't understand, though. At my running club, you can't wear headphones in a race.
Maybe it's for safety. You need to hear the other runners.
That's true. So for my half marathon — no music, just my breathing. [laugh]
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: which rule in your country do you think is unfair — and which one do you really like?
And be honest — do you ever bend the rules? See you next time!
Bye for now!
